chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Wasshash, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, who said:

I asked him about a woman upon whom death is approaching, and she has with her only one other woman; is her testimony valid or not? He said: 'The testimony of women is valid in the case of the 'Manfus (one who is free to give testimony, typically a male) and the 'Udhrah (a woman who is secluded or has no male guardian present).'

key_terms.الْمَنفُوسِ: The free person (male) who is eligible to give testimony
key_terms.وَالْعُذْرَةِ: The secluded woman (often one without a male guardian)
key_terms.يَحْضُرُهَا الْمَوْتُ: Upon whom death is approaching / dying

ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of a dying woman valid if she is with only one other woman?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, the Imam clarifies that a single woman’s testimony is sufficient in cases of 'Manfus' (typically referring to childbirth or midwifery matters) and 'Udhrah' (often interpreted as the private parts or specific intimate contexts), highlighting the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence regarding female witnesses. This ruling underscores the practical necessity of relying on women’s testimony in domestic and medical spheres where male witnesses may be absent, a principle deeply rooted in the Imams' pragmatic approach to evidence. The hadith serves as a key precedent for expanding the scope of valid female testimony beyond the traditional four-witness requirement in specific legal domains.
